abstract: Across dog breeds, the inverse correlation between body size and lifespan is well documented, but its genetic basis remains poorly understood, in part because size and lifespan are confounded at the breed level. Here, we assembled the Cani-DNA discovery cohort of 540 dogs from 27 breeds, with 20 dogs per breed, genotyped by low-pass whole-genome sequencing and imputation. We performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of breed-average body weight, breed-median lifespan and individual age at death, and tested the age-at-death loci for replication in the GRLS replication cohort of 3,024 Golden Retrievers. The GWAS of breed-average body weight recovered established body-size loci, confirming that the cohort could detect known associations. Of the 69 breed-weight loci, 30 were shared with breed-median lifespan, and at all of them the allele increasing body weight was associated with shorter lifespan. At the individual level, age at death, with breed-average body weight as a covariate, identified loci distinct from all breed-level loci. Three of them, the CDH4, TSHZ3 and TSC22D2 loci, replicated in the GRLS replication cohort. In humans, CDH4 and TSHZ3 have been implicated in longevity, and the region orthologous to the TSC22D2 locus has been associated with markers of biological ageing. Together, these results identify genetic variation associated with the lifespan of individual dogs beyond breed body size, and support the dog as a model in which genetic leads on ageing can be identified.
